stimulus.text:
Population of the United States, counted by the federal census:

| Year | Population |
| --- | --- |
| 1800 | 5,308,483 |
| 1820 | 9,638,453 |
| 1840 | 17,069,453 |

Miles of railroad track in operation: 23 miles in 1830 and 2,818 miles in 1840.

Source: United States census counts, 1800–1840; National Bureau of Economic Research, Business Annals, railroad mileage.
stimulus.source_note: Population from United States census counts, 1800-1840; railroad mileage from National Bureau of Economic Research, Business Annals (23 miles in 1830; 2,818 miles in 1840).

source: original; data from United States census counts and National Bureau of Economic Research, Business Annals
stem: By 1840 the nation held three times as many people and far more railroad miles than in 1800. Why did that rapid growth make the slavery question harder to settle?

options.text: Growth ended the cotton trade, so the South had nothing left to defend
options.misconception: The cotton trade grew with the nation, so the South had more, not less, to defend.

options.text: Each new territory forced a fresh decision about slavery's spread
Railroads let Congress ban slavery everywhere at once
options.misconception: Congress passed no such ban, and railroads do not make laws.

options.text: Population growth made voters stop caring about slavery
options.misconception: Growth sharpened the fight, as the Missouri crisis and later debates showed.

rationales.A: Cotton kept growing through the whole period. The South defended slavery more fiercely, not less.
rationales.B: Growth meant new land and new states. Every new territory raised the same question the Missouri Compromise had only postponed.
rationales.C: Railroads carry freight, not laws. No Congress of this period banned slavery everywhere.
rationales.D: Voters cared more, not less. Each new territory made the slavery question a live election issue.
rationales.general:
1. Follow the growth. More people and more land meant new territories asking to join the Union.
2. Ask what each new territory forced. Every admission raised the same question: would slavery spread there or not?
3. Name the pattern. The Missouri Compromise had settled one case, not the question, so growth kept reopening it.
Background: The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, and drew a line at 36 degrees 30 minutes.
Remember: when growth keeps adding new cases, one compromise cannot settle the question for good.
